6.27.m:
Mahādeva said:
The gift of water is supreme, always the best among gifts; / therefore one should cause stepped wells, wells, and tanks to be made.
Wells with flowing water continually destroy half the sin / of a man who has acted wrongfully, once he is well-engaged [in righteousness].
And he delivers his lineage in whose excavated reservoir / cows, vipras, and virtuous men always drink.
For him whose water remains in the summer season, O Nārada, / he is never overtaken in an impassable, harsh calamity.
And I will declare the virtues traditionally known of tanks that are constructed: / he who possesses a tank is worshiped everywhere in the three worlds.
Or rather, one should recognize a tank as the home of friends, increasing mutual friendship, / and the best producer of renown.
Wise men call a well-constructed tank in a region, in the midst of fields, a great refuge, / the fruit of dharma, wealth, and desire.
One should perceive a tank [as a shelter] for the four kinds of living beings; / and all tanks bestow supreme welfare.
Gods, men, gandharvas, ancestors, nāgas, rākṣasas, / and unmoving beings resort to a reservoir of water.
Where water remains in a tank during the rainy season, / the fruit of an agnihotra sacrifice accrues to him; of this there is no doubt.
For him whose water remains during autumn and winter, / he obtains the fruit of [gifting] a thousand cows; of this there is no doubt.
If water remains even in spring and summer, / wise men declare the fruit to be equal to an Atirātra and a horse sacrifice.
Now listen to the benefits in the planting of these trees: / O great sage, both the past and future ancestral lines of his father
the planter of trees delivers; therefore one should plant trees. / These trees become his sons and grandsons; of this there is no doubt.
He, gone to the other world, also attains imperishable worlds. / Trees worship all the hosts of gods with their flowers, and likewise the ancestors with their leaves,
and all guests with their shade. / Kinnaras, serpents, rākṣasas, gods, gandharvas, and mortals,
as well as hosts of sages, resort to trees; / blossoming and bearing fruit, they gratify human beings here.
In this world and in the next, they are regarded as his sons in accordance with dharma. / Those who excavate tanks, plant trees, and those twice-born who perform iṣṭi sacrifices—
these do not fall from heaven, nor do those others who speak truth. / Truth alone is the supreme brahman; truth alone is the supreme asceticism;
truth alone is the supreme sacrifice; truth alone is the supreme scripture. / Truth is awake among the gods; truth is the supreme state.
Austerity, sacrifices, merit, and the worship of gods and sages, / the primordial ordinance, and knowledge—everything is established on truth.
Truth is the sacrifice, the gift, the mantras, and the goddess Sarasvatī; / the performance of vows is likewise truth, and the syllable Om is truth itself.
By truth the wind blows; by truth the sun burns; / by truth fire scorches; and heaven stands through truth.
The worship of all the gods, bathing in all the sacred fords, / and one speaks truth in the world—he attains everything, without doubt.
A thousand horse sacrifices and truth were placed on a balance: / truth alone excels above all sacrifices whatsoever.
By truth the gods are pleased, as well as the ancestors and sages. / They call truth the supreme dharma; they call truth the supreme state;
they call truth the supreme brahman; therefore I speak truth to you. / Sages devoted to truth, having performed severe austerity,
delighting in true dharma, perfected beings, went hence to heaven, / surrounded on all sides by aerial cars resounding with hosts of apsarases.
And truth must always be spoken; there is nothing higher than truth. / In the deep, vast, perfected, true sacred ford that is a pure heart,

those endowed with self-control should bathe; that bath is considered supreme. / Mortals who do not speak untruth, whether for their own sake, for another's sake, or for the sake of a son, / those men go to heaven.
Vedas, sacrifices, and mantras reside continually in vipras; / they do not shine in those who have abandoned truth; therefore one should practice truth.

Nārada said:
Tell me once more specifically the fruit of austerities / and the power of austerity of all the castes, especially of brāhmaṇas.

[Mahādeva said:]
I shall declare the austerity and meditation that accomplishes all desires and goals, / difficult to practice for the twice-born; listen to it as I speak.
Austerity indeed is declared supreme; through austerity one finds reward. / One who is constantly devoted to austerity rejoices with the gods.
Through austerity heaven is attained; through austerity renown is attained. / Through austerity one attains liberation; through austerity one finds greatness.
Wealth of knowledge and direct realization, good fortune, and beauty as well— / through austerity one obtains everything, whatever one desires in the mind.
Those who have not performed austerity never go to the world of Brahmā. / Whatever enterprise a person undertakes and performs austerity for,

he obtains all of that both in the next world and here, O mortal. / A drinker of liquor, an adulterer, a killer of a brāhmaṇa, or a violator of a guru’s bed— / through austerity crosses over all and is liberated from everything.
Even the lord of all, Sthāṇu, and eternal Viṣṇu, / Brahmā, the fire god, Indra, and whoever else are endowed with austerity,
as well as eighty-six thousand celibate sages / rejoice in heaven through austerity, joined together with the deities.
Through austerity kingship is attained. Formerly, Indra and all the gods, / sustaining all through austerity, bestowed sustenance day after day.
The two deities, the sun and the moon, devoted to the welfare of all worlds, / and likewise the lunar mansions and the planets, shine through austerity alone.
And everything is approached through austerity, and one enjoys all happiness. / One who performs austerity in the forest, eating roots and fruits of the woods,
and one who studies the Veda in the beginning—[their merit] would be equal in austerity, O sage. / The merit that a best of the twice-born obtains from teaching the Veda,
he enjoys double that reward from the recitation and silent repetition of its chapter. / Just as the world becomes lightless without the moon and the sun,
so indeed the Purāṇa should be meditated upon from this, O great sage. / Performing austerity, one who retains knowledge according to the scripture,
and awakens the world, is on that account the most venerable guru. / And among all worthy recipients, the knower of the Purāṇa is the supreme recipient.
Because he protects against falling [into hell], he is called a worthy recipient. / Wealth, grain, gold, or various garments—
those who give them to a worthy recipient attain the supreme state. / And cows, or female buffaloes, elephants, and handsome horses—
hear the fruit of the merit of one who offers these to the foremost [recipient]! / He obtains the imperishable fruit of a horse sacrifice among all the worlds.
He who gives him the earth, cultivated, fruitful, and auspicious, / delivers his ancestors, ten preceding and ten succeeding generations.
And he goes to the world of Viṣṇu by means of a celestial aerial chariot. / The gods do not derive such satisfaction from sacrifices, nor from sprinklings,
nor from offerings and flower-worship, as from recitations of the book. / But one who has a book of dharma prepared in a sanctuary of Viṣṇu,
or again in that of the Goddess, of Śambhu, of Gaṇeśa, or of the Sun, / that mortal attains the fruit of a royal consecration and a horse sacrifice.
From the legendary histories and the Purāṇas, the reading of the book is meritorious; / one obtains all desires and pierces the realm of the sun.
and having broken through the solar world, he goes to the world of Brahmā. / Having stayed there for hundreds of kalpas, he becomes a king on the face of the earth.
Whatever fruit is declared for a thousand horse sacrifices, / he who recites the Jaya before the deity attains that reward.

Therefore, by every effort, the recitation of the book / of legendary history and Purāṇa should be performed in the auspicious sanctuary of Viṣṇu; / nothing else is so pleasing to Viṣṇu and likewise to the other dwellers of heaven.

6.28.m: Mahādeva said: / In this regard, they also cite this ancient legendary history, / the supreme, meritorious Purāṇa that removes all sin and brings auspiciousness.
And this narrative of the worlds was spoken to me, O divine sage, / by Kumāra, the son of Brahmā, having bowed to the Grandfather.
Sanatkumāra said: / I went to see Dharmarāja and was joyfully honored [by him] / with Vedic hymns and supreme devotion; and I was invited to an easy seat by him.
As I sat there, something exceedingly wonderful was seen by me. / In a golden aerial chariot with an altar-platform made of cat’s-eye gem,
adorned with jewels and pearls, and beautified by clusters of tiny bells, / a man arrived there from his seat, O best of deities.
Seeing him, the all-pervading Dharma himself stood up in haste, / grasped him by the right hand, and honored him with respectful water.
Having smelled his head, the lord of gods placed him in front, and thereupon, / having worshipped him, Dharma spoke this word:
“A hearty welcome to you, O beholder of dharma! I am pleased with the sight of you. / Remain near me and tell me some wisdom.
You will go again to that abode where Brahmā resides.” / And when this was said, another man, seated in an excellent aerial chariot,
a divine man, arrived where the king of dharma was standing. / Seated in the aerial chariot, he was honored by [Dharma], who was bowed with modesty,
and speaking conciliation beforehand just as to the previous man: / “What action was done by this person, with whom you are exceedingly pleased?
Here curiosity has arisen in me, since worship was indeed performed by yourself, / directly, filled with wonder, immediately thereafter.
Just so, worship was performed for this second man. / I deemed these two best of excellent men in the aerial chariots to be of auspicious deeds,
since you yourself perform worship to these two for the sake of dharma, / yet you are constantly worshipped day and night by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others.
Whose supreme merit is of such a kind? What action did these two perform? / Let it be told to me, O omniscient one, how they obtained celestial reward.”
Hearing that, he said to me: “Hear the deed done by these two, / by doing which they came here as worthy ones; hear that, O highly intelligent one!
Dharma said: / There is a city renowned on earth named Vaidiśa. / There ruled an earth-protector famous as Dharāpāla.
At a certain time long ago, the Goddess angrily cursed her attendant: / ‘Because another woman was brought to my husband without me,
therefore you shall be a jackal for twelve years!’ / Addressed thus, he roamed the surface of the earth as a jackal.
‘At the confluence of the Vetasī and the Vetravatī, famed in the world, / the end of the curse will come, O son,’ so it had been declared by the Mountain’s daughter.
And there, having fasted to death, he abandoned his life-breaths in that sacred place; / assuming a body of celestial form, he went into the presence of Viṣṇu.
Seeing that great wonder there, the king Dharāpāla, / having constructed a sanctuary for Viṣṇu, abandoned his life in that sacred place.
Assuming a body of celestial form, he installed that Lord, / having appointed all the men in that city to look after it.
The auspicious sanctuary of Viṣṇu in that village was always full of people; / and having honored the multitude of brāhmaṇas and others,
Having honoured the reciter especially, who knows the legendary histories and Purāṇas, / the best among the twice-born, preeminent in learning, the one of great intellect [attains fulfillment].
and having also properly worshipped the book with perfumes, flowers, and the like, / that king, endowed with humility, then addressed that reciter:
‘This sanctuary of Viṣṇu has been constructed before you, / and this assembly of the four castes is also eager to listen.’”
“Stay here, O best of the twice-born! Undertake the reading of the book / for a full year, O brāhmaṇa, receiving an unsurpassed livelihood.
And here I will give a hundred gold niṣkas, and then another [gift], / when the year is complete, O best of the twice-born, for my own welfare.”
In this way the meritorious reading of the book was begun there; / and no sooner had the year passed, O best of sages,
than by the exhaustion of his lifespan he went the way of all mortals, / and by me, Viṣṇu, a celestial chariot was indeed sent for him from heaven.
Such is the reward of actions, a meritorious work termed a narrative; / heard from the Padma Purāṇa, it is greatly meritorious, purifying, and destructive of sin.
Indeed, such satisfaction does not arise in all the gods here / through offerings of perfumes and flowers as it does from hearing a Purāṇa.
From the gift of articles of gold, jewels, and the like, or of garments entirely, / or of villages and towns, satisfaction surely does not arise,
as delight would arise in all the heaven-dwellers from hearing dharma, / in the hearing of legendary histories and Purāṇas, O best of sages.
So too great delight would arise in me, when all desired ends are achievable; / great delight would be mine in the giving away of a maiden [in marriage], O best of sages,
yet even that does not please [me] so much as from the reading of the book. / Now, what is the use of speaking much? Nothing else brings me delight
save a meritorious narration, O brāhmaṇa: this is proclaimed as a secret. / And this other brāhmaṇa, a best of men who came here,
and followed along by chance to the supreme hearing of dharma— / having heard, devotion to the Supreme Self arose in him through faith.
Having circumambulated that noble reader, / this brāhmaṇa, O best of sages, gave a māṣaka of gold.
He never made any other gift, his mind being seized by greed; / yet the attainment of fruit arose for him from a gift given to a worthy recipient—there is no doubt.
Thus the deed of both of these has been told in this manner, O great sage.
Mahādeva said: / Those wise persons who hear this glorification of the meritorious deed— / no misfortune ever arises for them in birth after birth.

6.29.m: Mahādeva said: / Now I shall tell something else; listen, O best of divine sages: / the glorification of Gopīcandana, as it has been seen and heard by me.
Whether a brāhmaṇa, a vaiśya, a śūdra, or a twice-born, / one whose body is smeared with Gopīcandana is freed from the murder of a brāhmaṇa.
He who makes a tilaka mark made of Gopīcandana / is freed from the sins of drinking liquor and the like—there is no doubt here.
With limbs smeared with Gopīcandana, a Vaiṣṇava devoted to Viṣṇu / would be thoroughly freed from all sins, just as with the water of the Gaṅgā.
A killer of a brāhmaṇa, a drinker of liquor, a thief of gold as well, / or one who defiles the bed of his guru, whether a śūdra or a twice-born,
is instantly freed from sin accrued over hundreds of births. / The twelvefold tilaka is declared especially for everyone.
It should be applied by Vaiṣṇavas and by brāhmaṇas who desire prosperity: / on the forehead it should be rod-shaped, but on the chest lotus-shaped;
at the base of the arm resembling a bamboo leaf; another [has] the shape of a lamp; / four disc [marks] high up at the base of the right arm;
two name-seals lower down, and one conch between them; / then on both sides in the middle one should wear two lotuses each.
On the left also, four conches and two name-seals as before, / according to the distinction of one disc and two maces on each of them;
on the forehead one mace, and likewise on the heart a name-seal; / three variegated [marks] each, and two branching marks on both in the middle;
on the chest, on the flank above the breast, maces and lotuses as on the arms; / three and four discs below both earlobes;
and one each in the other tilakas one should apply. / The seal born of tradition, however, should be worn according to exemplary conduct,
or it may be worn as one pleases; there is no strict rule in that regard. / From a cāṇḍāla upwards, they are purified merely by wearing the tilaka.
Worse than a cāṇḍāla I consider one who reviles Vaiṣṇavas. / And he [the Vaiṣṇava] is to be known as equal to Viṣṇu; no doubt should be entertained here.
A brāhmaṇa who is a Vaiṣṇava, intent on meditations upon Viṣṇu— / no difference is to be known in him: he is verily Viṣṇu in this world.
A brāhmaṇa bearing the conch and disc, devoted to the study of the Veda, / is indeed Nārāyaṇa: so it is read in the Veda itself.
A brāhmaṇa bearing the branded disc is a purifier of the purifiers of assemblies; / filled with devotion to him, O brāhmaṇa, one is released from great sins.
Wearing a garland of tulasī leaves or one made from tulasī wood, / a brāhmaṇa would indeed become a sharer in liberation—there is no doubt.
Because a brāhmaṇa is a form of Viṣṇu, a Vaiṣṇava is commemorated here as such. / He upon whose death there is a tilaka made of Gopīcandana,
mounting a celestial chariot, goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu. / In the Kali age, O Nārada, I will speak of the Gopīcandana tilaka:
Those best of men who apply it never meet with misfortune anywhere. / Wearing a conch and likewise a disc on both the right and left
hand especially, one is released from great sins. / Those who are intent on drinking liquor, and those who are killers of women and children,
those who approach forbidden women who are seen on earth, O brāhmaṇa— / by the mere sight of devotees, liberation is theirs; there is no doubt.
In this saṃsāra of worthless essence, whence indeed do Vaiṣṇavas come? / I myself have become a Vaiṣṇava through the grace of devotion to Viṣṇu.
For those residing in Kāśī, constantly chanting ‘Rāma, Rāma’ here, / through that combination of merit and the rest, one becomes Śiva; there is no doubt here.

6.30.m: Nārada said: / O brāhmaṇa, tell me the excellent rite of the lamp named ‘Yearly’, / the glorification of that which is the foremost of all observances,
by which all vows are truly performed—there is no doubt— / and there is the flourishing of all desires and the destruction of all sins.
Mahādeva said: / I will speak to you, O divine sage, a sin-destroying secret, / hearing which a killer of a brāhmaṇa, a killer of a cow, a slayer of a friend, one who defiles his guru's bed,
a betrayer of trust, a cruel-hearted person, attains eternal liberation; / delivering a hundred families, he goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Therefore I shall explain the unsurpassed lamp observance: / the rite of a year's duration and its glorification as well.
In the first month of winter, on reaching the auspicious eleventh day [of the fortnight], / rising at the brāhma hour, free from desire and anger,
at sacred waters of river confluences, in ponds, and in rivers, / or at home, with self-restraint, one should perform a bath.
“I have bathed in all sacred waters; grant me that bath always.”
he should then worship the lord, the god Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa, / having bathed him with the fivefold ambrosia, and then with fragrant water:
“You are bathed together with Lakṣmī, O god of gods, lord of the world! / Deliver me, O lord of the gods, from the terrible bondage of saṃsāra!”
Then one should worship god Janārdana along with Lakṣmī / with devotion, using Vedic as well as Purāṇic mantras,
or again with the Puruṣa Sūkta beginning with 'Ato devāḥ' along with scents and the like: / 'Homage to Matsya, the god! Homage indeed to Kūrma, the god!
Homage to the boar god! Homage indeed to Narasiṃha! / Homage be to the Buddha god! And homage, homage to Kalkin!

Homage be to the Rāma god! Homage to you, Viṣṇu, the god! / Homage to you, the Self of all!'—saying 'to the head' one should worship him; / or one should worship Hari with names beginning with Keśava.
'Divine sap of trees, fragrant, sweet-smelling, and pure, / this incense, O God, Lord of gods, homage to you! May it be accepted.'
The mantra for the incense: / 'The lamp destroys darkness; the lamp bestows radiance. / Therefore, by the offering of a lamp, may Janārdana be pleased with me.'
The mantra for the lamp: / 'This food-offering consisting of grain, O God of gods, Lord of the world, / take it along with Lakṣmī, supreme, excellent nectar.'
The mantra for the food-offering: / Then one should devoutly offer the arghya, having thus meditated on Janārdana, / holding fruit in the hand and taking water in a conch shell:
'Whatever sin has been committed by me in a thousand other births, / may all of that come to destruction through your grace, O Keśava.'

Thus ends the argha mantra.
Then one should bring a new, clean pot filled with ghee,
or else filled with oil, before Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa.
Upon it one should place a copper or clay vessel; / and in that vessel one should lay a wick equal to nine threads.
Then, having placed the jar firmly motionless, one should kindle the lamp; / having worshipped it with flowers, scents, and the like, one who is pure should then make the solemn resolve,
with this mantra, O divine seer: / 'In windless abodes, Desire, the sole sovereign ruler / of what has been and what is to be, shines forth.
This lamp has been prepared by me for the duration of a year / as an unbroken fire-sacrifice. May Keśava be pleased with me.'
Then, having conquered his senses, intent upon the knowledge of the Śruti, / he should not converse with fallen sinners, nor with heretical men.
At night there should be keeping vigil with song, dance, instrumental music, and the like, / as well as through various sacred recitations, discourses on dharma, and fasts.
Then, at the time of daybreak, having performed his morning rites, / he should feed brāhmaṇas with devotion and honor them according to his capacity.
And having broken his fast himself, he should salute them and bid them farewell. / In this way, firm in his vow day and night for the duration of a year,
[he should prepare] a lamp with a pala of gold, or with half of that; / and the wick is said to be of silver, weighing two palas or half of that;
likewise a jar filled with clarified butter together with a copper vessel; / and the god Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa should be made of gold according to capacity
by a devoted man desiring the gateway to liberation. / Then the wise person should invite brāhmaṇas, the best of virtuous men:
in the best case twelve brāhmaṇas, in the intermediate case six, / or otherwise he should have three, or a single ritually active twice-born.
A peaceful twice-born accompanied by his wife, particularly observant of rites, / knowledgeable in legendary history and the Purāṇas, knowing dharma, and gentle,
devoted to parents, dedicated to his guru, a worshipper of gods and brāhmaṇas— / by the procedure of giving foot-water and arghya, with clothes, ornaments, and adornments,
having devoutly worshipped that one [brāhmaṇa] together with his wife as before, / [and having placed] god Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, along with the lamp and wick,

upon a copper vessel together with the jar of clarified butter, / he should then give it to the brāhmaṇa, having meditated upon supreme Nārāyaṇa / with this mantra, O divine seer, which I declare to you:

'In the cycle of worldly existence enveloped by the darkness of ignorance, it is the destroyer of sin, / the bestower of knowledge, and the granter of liberation; therefore it has been given by me, O sinless one.'

Thus ends the lamp mantra.
And having given a priestly gift to a brahmin with devotion according to one's means,
one should then feed the brahmins with ghee, rice pudding, and sweetmeats.
He should then clothe that twice-born together with his wife with garments, / and should give a bed furnished with accessories and a milch cow with her calf.
To them he should give a priestly gift according to his wealth; / and he should feed and honor friends, relatives, and kin.
In this manner he should celebrate a great festival at the conclusion of the lamp vow; / then, having bowed down, he should ask for forgiveness and dismiss them.
When this is done, whatever merit is [obtained] by those [observances] connected with the solstices and equinoxes, / that fruit of the so-called yearly lamp is attained by men.
And whatever merit is gained by monthly vows, that merit is attained by men / by the performance of the vow of the yearly lamp.
Whatever [fruit is obtained] by numerous vows of gifts and vows of yoga, / that fruit he fully obtains when the yearly lamp has been offered.
Whatever fruit a wise man obtains from gifts of cows, land, and gold, and especially houses, / that fruit accrues to the giver of a lamp.
The giver of a lamp obtains radiance; the giver of a lamp obtains imperishable wealth; / the giver of a lamp obtains knowledge; the giver of a lamp obtains supreme happiness.
And from the gift of a lamp one obtains good fortune, extremely spotless learning, / health, and supreme prosperity; there is no doubt in this.
The giver of a lamp obtains an auspicious wife endowed with all good marks, / sons, grandsons, great-grandsons, and imperishable lineage.
A brāhmaṇa attains supreme knowledge, a kṣatriya an excellent kingdom, / a vaiśya all wealth and cattle, and a śūdra happiness.
An unmarried girl also obtains a husband endowed with all good marks, / supreme longevity, and abundant sons and grandsons.
A young woman never sees widowhood at any time, / nor does she experience separation, by the power of the gift of a lamp.
Neither mental distresses nor physical diseases arise from the gift of a lamp; / the frightened is freed from fear, and one bound is released from bondage.
One devoted to the vow of the lamp is freed from sins / such as killing a brāhmaṇa; there is no doubt in this, just as is the word of Brahmā.
The cāndrāyaṇa and kṛcchra penances have indeed been performed, without doubt, / by him by whom the perpetual yearly lamp of Hari has been kindled.
They are fortunate, they are great souls, the fruit of life has been attained by them, / by whom, having worshipped Hari with devotion, the yearly lamp has been established.
Even those who here watch the trimming of the wick of the lamp / go to the supreme abode which is difficult to attain even for the gods.
Those who constantly add oil and a wick according to their capacity / to the lamp go to the supreme destination.
If one is unable to rekindle a lamp that is going out / but tells other people, they too share in that fruit.
Even by begging for oil little by little for the sake of the lamp / and making a lamp for Viṣṇu, merit is obtained by him.
Even a low man who, with folded hands, / sees a lamp being kindled for Viṣṇu attains the world of Viṣṇu.
Whoever directs his mind toward the kindling of a lamp, or does so himself, / freed from all sins, attains the world of Viṣṇu.
On this subject they also relate this ancient legendary history, / by the mere hearing of which one is freed from all sins.
On the charming bank of the Sarasvatī there was a famous place called Siddhāśrama; / there formerly lived a twice-born named Kapila, a knower of the Veda.
Devoted to vows and fasting, poor, and a learned scholar of the Vedas, / he maintained his family by begging for alms.
Through vows, fasts, and observances, he worshipped Viṣṇu; / having worshipped Viṣṇu according to rule, he constantly lit a lamp.
Bringing that oil and worshipping Keśava in his home, / he would kindle the lamp with supreme devotion to please Hari.
While the great-souled Kapila lived in this manner, / a cat with sharp fangs constantly ate mice [there].
He went there day and night to feed upon mice; / fixing his concentration, he always sat before Nārāyaṇa for the sake of food.
Many mice were eaten by him in the house of the twice-born man— / those who came for the oil and to snatch away the wick.
Intent in his contemplation, he devoured those very mice. / As time went by while things proceeded in this way,
on an Ekādaśī, that brāhmaṇa Kapila, pure in his own house, / together with his wife and fasting, worshipped Acyuta.
Then, intent on hymns of praise and dancing, he kept a night vigil; / but when midnight arrived, the twice-born man was overcome by sleep.
And the cat arrived there, sharp-fanged and light of step; / stationed constantly in a corner of the house, he watched the food offering.
He caught sight of a little mouse who had come to drink the oil, / intent on stealing the wick when the lamp grew faint in its brilliance.
Leaping up and pouncing with its paws, [the mouse] then entered a hole; / by its foot, the wick of the lamp was raised up brightly.
And the oil vessel was tilted, so that a great light shone forth; / the brāhmaṇa also awoke, casting off deluding sleep.
And the mouse-devouring cat also remained awake that whole night. / Then, when clear dawn broke, the twice-born man performed his daily rites.
And then the brāhmaṇa broke his fast together with his kinsmen. / As the great-souled Kapila lived in this manner,
sons and grandsons were born to him, along with unsurpassed wealth and grain; / he attained health, supreme prosperity, and great fortune.
By the power of the lamp-vow, Kapila attained liberation; / having pierced the holy orbs of the sun and the moon,

the Supreme Self placed him in the form of the flame of a lamp. / The mouse, too, died in due course of time inside the hole;

mounting an excellent celestial chariot, she went to the realm of Viṣṇu. / And at the end of his time, the cat also died and went to heaven;
mounting an excellent celestial chariot attended by gods and Gandharvas, / surrounded by Apsarases, and joined by hosts of Vidyādharas,
praised, of great splendor, with auspicious shouts of victory and the like, / and praised by the celestial serpents, he went to the realm of Viṣṇu.
Having enjoyed extensive pleasures for thousands of tens of millions of kalpas / and hundreds of tens of millions of kalpas, he then became a king on earth,
named Sudharma, righteous in soul, a worshipper of gods and brāhmaṇas, / handsome, fortunate, and possessed of great strength and valor.
His most beloved wife was endowed with all auspicious marks, / devoted to her husband, virtuous, and named Rūpasundarī.
Among all women she was indeed the most fortunate, / and many sons were born to them, as well as a host of daughters.
As the couple thus sported with mutual affection, / the month of Kārttika arrived, which awakens the eyes of Hari.
In that month lamps are lit by those devoted to Nārāyaṇa, / and severe penances such as Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa, vows, and observances
are performed by devotees of Viṣṇu who are terrified of the fear of worldly existence. / Then, when the Prabodhinī [Ekādaśī] arrived, the king spoke to the queen:
"O auspicious one, today is the holy Prabodhinī [springing from] the navel-lotus of Viṣṇu; / fasting and with subdued senses, I shall perform worship today.
Having bathed at the holy site of Puṣkara, / I shall worship the lotus-eyed Acyuta, the Lord of gods, Janārdana together with Lakṣmī."

Hearing this wish of her husband, she who was intent on his pleasure and welfare,
that sweetly smiling lady spoke a secret word to her husband.
Rūpasundarī said: / "O king, a desire has also arisen in my heart, / and a longing for form and beauty dwells within my heart.
I wish to go with you to Puṣkara, the foremost holy ford." / Then the king went with her to Puṣkara,
accompanied by hosts of elephants, horses, and chariots, and by priests; / then, having bathed, meditating, and offering libations to the ancestors and the gods,
he worshipped the lotus-eyed Acyuta, the Lord of gods, / in that place crowded with rows of lamps, enchanting on all sides.
There in the temple of the deity he saw a cat painted [on a wall]; / seeing it, the king remembered his former action and birth;
looking upon the lotus-face of his beloved, he smiled. / Rūpasundarī said: / "Looking directly at my face, my lord, what is the reason for your smile?"
Delighted in soul, he recounted the fruit of past actions. / The king said: / "O queen, previously I was a cat in the house of a brāhmaṇa;
hundreds and thousands of mice were eaten there by me. / Because the lamp in front of Nārāyaṇa was preserved through that,
even though done unwittingly, O queen, the fruit of that act was attained by me: / having attained the realm of Viṣṇu, I have now attained kingship."
Rūpasundarī said: / "I too have remembered my previous birth: / I also was a small mouse in the house of the brāhmaṇa.
During Kārttika on the Prabodhinī, when the lamp had grown faint, / I came out of my hole to steal the tip of the wick.
Seeing the god Nārāyaṇa worshipped with flowers, / and the brāhmaṇa overcome with sleep, the wick was then pulled by me.
When you sprang up there, seizing the moment to catch me, / seeing you, I fled and entered the hole.
As I entered, the wick of the lamp was raised by my foot / and the oil vessel was tilted; thereby have I become a sharer in happiness.
Thus the lamp was brightened by me, O lord of kings; / and now I have attained supreme beauty and charm,
and you as my husband, as well as a kingdom, sons, and such happiness! / From lighting the lamp arose this extremely rare knowledge.
Therefore, with every effort, let both of us especially / perform the unsurpassed lamp-vow with supreme devotion!
This is the fruit obtained from that deed: sovereign power and other riches, / the memory of our previous birth, and the destruction of all sins.
Therefore, when the lamp-vow is performed by men with every effort, / accompanied by rules and mantras, its merit lasts as long as the moon, sun, and stars."

Hearing this word, the king then observed the vow of lamps
together with his beloved, endowed with perfect faith, O divine sage.
Having performed the lamp-vow at that holy ford of Puṣkara, the two / attained supreme liberation, difficult even for gods and demons to achieve.
Men on earth who listen to this glorification of the lamp, / freed from all sins, go to the dwelling place of Hari.

And whatever men or women, intent on devotion, perform it, / they, all freed from sin, attain the eternal Brahman.

This lamp-vow, which grants liberation, has been told to you, O learned one; / granting all happiness and auspicious, this great vow is for you.
Diseases of the eye, such as are born from the power of sin, are destroyed; / indeed, mental agonies and all physical diseases are destroyed in an instant upon doing it.
There is neither poverty, nor sorrow, nor delusion, nor confusion; / in his house, Lakṣmī arrives birth after birth, O brāhmaṇa!

6.31.m: Nārada said: / O God of gods, Lord of the world, grantor of fearlessness to devotees, / having shown compassion to me, tell of a vow, O Mahādeva!
The glorious Mahādeva said: / Formerly, there was a universal monarch named Hariścandra, lord of the earth; / pleased with him, Brahmā gave him an auspicious city that yielded every desire,
composed of all gems, divine, with radiance like the newly risen sun. / Residing there, the ruler of the earth protected the earth,
with its seven continents, through righteousness, like a father his own legitimate son. / Possessing abundant wealth and grain, the king had sons and grandsons.
Protecting that auspicious kingdom, he was struck by supreme wonder: / "Never before has such a kingdom belonged to anyone whatsoever;
nor has such a celestial vehicle been mounted by other men. / What particular deed in this world was done by which I have become like the king of the gods?"

Thus absorbed in thought, seated upon an excellent aerial chariot,
the excellent monarch saw Meru, the best of peaks.
There was that great-souled one, like a second sun, / seated on that best of mountains, upon a golden rocky slab—
the divine seer Sanatkumāra, devoted to the yoga of knowledge. / Seeing him, the king descended, wishing to ask about his wonder.
Delighted, he bowed to his feet, and was greeted with joy by him as well. / Seated comfortably, the king asked the foremost of sages:
"O Blessed One, such wealth as mine is hard to obtain in the world; / by what action is it obtained, and who was I in a previous birth?
Tell me all the truth, if I am worthy of your favor!" / Sanatkumāra said: "Listen, O king, I will tell the cause of the past event,
by performing which, in particular, favor was bestowed upon you. / In your previous birth, you were a noble vaiśya, truthful in speech, pure;
your own work was abandoned by you, and then you were abandoned by your kinsmen. / Your livelihood thus ruined, followed by your wife,
you set forth, abandoning your own people, desiring service from another; / but there was no employment given, as you were afflicted by famine at that time.
Then once, in a dense forest, seeing a lake with blooming lotuses, / the intention was made there: 'Let us two gather lotuses.'
Having said this much, taking those flowers step by step, / they reached the holy city named Varanasi, the auspicious.
Then, from the sale, no one bought any lotus. / Someone coming out of a monastery there remained right in the courtyard.
Entering that place, the sound of musical instruments was heard [by him]: / 'In what [place] is this sound of musical instruments heard?'

When asked thus, and when it was swiftly spoken by him, he set forth elsewhere—
the king of Kāśī indeed, and the renowned king Indradyumna.

He has a famed, virtuous daughter named Candrāvatī,
a fortunate woman who kept the fast on the auspicious Jayantī-Aṣṭamī.

That vaiśya came there, where that auspicious woman was staying;
his mind was pleased, and great joy came upon him then,

In that place, O god, you saw the sacrificial rite,
where the blessed Lord Hari is worshipped together with the sun.

With devotion to Him, an offering of flowers was made by you together with your wife,
and an expanse composed of flowers was likewise made there with the rest.

Seeing that, she was amazed: 'By whom was worship performed here?'
Having recognized that deed, all that was protected accordingly.

Then, well-pleased, she herself gave you much wealth;
wealth was not accepted by you, and you were invited for a meal.

No meal was taken, nor was wealth [accepted] by you then;
that sun, united with Viṣṇu, was worshipped in accordance with the rule.

Then at dawn, constantly watched over by her,
having put them all at ease, you departed as you wished.

Thus this merit was acquired by you in another birth,
and you reached dissolution according to the consequence of your own actions.

By that great merit a celestial chariot arrived then;
O king, that fruit produced in the previous birth is now being enjoyed.

Hariścandra said:
By what precise rule and in which month should that lunar day
be observed? Tell me that, if I am to be favored by you.

Sanatkumāra said:
Listen attentively, O king, to what is being related by me to you,
concerning the dark eighth of the month of Śrāvaṇa, O ruler of men.

If Rohiṇī should be joined with it, that lunar day is named Jayantī;
again and again, O great king, it becomes the cause of birth [freed from sorrow].

I shall describe its ritual procedure as declared to me by Brahmā,
by performing which, freed from sin, one goes to Viṣṇu's realm.

Having fasted and then bathed with black sesame seeds,
one should install an unblemished jar provided with the five gems.

Diamond, pearl, beryl, topaz, and sapphire—
the five gems are commended [thus], so Kātyāyana said.

Upon it one should place a golden vessel endowed with auspicious marks;
one should place there a golden image of Yaśodā, Nanda's housewife,

giving her breast to her son, her face filled with wonder,
while he, drinking one breast of his mother, touches the other with his hand,

gazing upon his mother with love, delighting her again and again.
One should cause the god to be fashioned of gold, as far as one's capacity extends.

It should be made of the measure of two niṣkas, if the capacity exists;
it should be made with three metals or else with gold.

Likewise one should make Rohiṇī of gold, and the moon of silver;
the moon should be merely the size of a thumb, and Rohiṇī four finger-breadths.

One should place two earrings on the ears and a neck-ornament upon the neck;
having fashioned Govinda, the lord of the universe, together with his mother in this way,

having bathed them with milk and other substances, one should anoint them with sandalwood paste,
[and adorn them with] a pair of white garments, an umbrella, and floral garlands.

With various food-offerings, confections, and also various kinds of fruit,
one should arrange lamps there, adorned within a flower pavilion.

A devout person should have songs, dances, and instrumental music performed by learned men.
Having thus carried out the rite according to the extent of one's wealth,
one should subsequently worship the preceptor and conclude the worship there.

6.32.m:
Mahādeva said:
Having seen the Lord of a Hundred Sacrifices accomplished, with gifts to priests completed,
Maghavan, with a purpose arisen in his mind, questioned Bṛhaspati:

O blessed one, by what gift does happiness increase in every way?
Tell me that, O great ascetic, which is imperishable and of great worth.

Addressed thus by Indra, that god of gods and family priest,
the very wise Bṛhaspati, smiling at him, said:

The gift of gold, the gift of cattle, and the gift of land, O Vāsava—
he who bestows these is completely freed from all sins.

Gold, silver, cloth, and gems and jewels, O Vāsava—
everything has been given by him who bestows the earth.

Having given earth ploughed by the share, sown with seed, garlanded with crops,
as long as light is made by the sun, so long is one honored in heaven.

Whatever sin a man commits, distressed by livelihood,
he is purified by a gift of land even of the measure of a cow's hide.

Here a staff is ten cubits; thirty staffs are a nivartana;
ten of those are a cow's hide: this is the definition of a cow's hide, O Indra.

Where a thousand cows along with a bull can stand unconstrained,
cows that have calved with young calves, that is remembered as a cow's hide.

If one gives to a brāhmaṇa endowed with virtues, possessing ascetic power, with senses restrained,
as long as the earth stands bounded by the ocean, so long will his fruit be unending.

Just as a drop of oil fallen into water spreads out, O Śakra,
even so a gift made of land spreads from crop to crop.

Just as seeds grow when scattered over the surface of the earth,
even so desires sprout forth, joined with the gift of land.

Givers of food are constantly happy; a giver of clothing becomes handsome;
that man becomes a giver of all things, who bestows the earth.

Just as a cow gives milk, letting forth milk to maintain her calf,
even so the earth, given, O thousand-eyed one, supports the giver of land.

A conch, a throne, a parasol, excellent horses, and excellent elephants—
heaven is the fruit of the merit of the gift of land, O Puraṃdara.

The sun, Varuṇa, Fire, Brahmā, the moon, the eater of oblations,
and the blessed trident-handed Lord all applaud the giver of land.

The fathers clap their hands, the grandfathers declare:
'A giver of land is born in our family; he will be our deliverer!'

They declare three supreme gifts: cattle, the earth, and Sarasvatī;
these deliver from hell through muttering, sowing, and milking.

Through the learned, the supporters among brāhmaṇas, they carry one across misfortune.
Covered, the givers of clothing go; naked go those who give no clothing.

Sated go the givers of food; hungry go those who give no food.
All the ancestors desire [this], afraid with fear of hell:

'That son who goes to Gayā will be our deliverer.'
Many sons are to be desired, in the hope that even one might go to Gayā,

or might sacrifice with a horse sacrifice, or release a blue bull.
One that is reddish in color, but white at the tip of its tail,

white in hooves and horns, is called a blue bull.
A blue [bull] with a white tail, which raises up water—

by him the ancestors are gratified for sixty thousand years;
and whatever mud is borne upon its horns, his lineage stands delivered.

And his ancestors feed upon the radiant realm of the moon.
It belonged to King Dilīpa, to Nṛga, and to Nahuṣa,

and to other rulers of men, yet none takes it away.
Land has been given by many kings, beginning with Sagara;

whosever the land is at any time, his is the fruit at that time.
Whether a slayer of a brāhmaṇa, a slayer of a woman, a slayer of a child, or an outcaste—
or the slayer of a hundred thousand cows—such is his evil deed! / Whoever seizes land, whether given by himself or given by another,
becomes a worm in excrement and is cooked together with his ancestors. / The giver of land resides in heaven for sixty thousand years;
the one who takes it away, and the one who consents to it, will go to hell for just as long. / There is no other possessor of merit or sin [greater] than the giver of land and the stealer of land.
The two of them abide—the one above, the other below—until the dissolution of all beings.
Gold is the first offspring of Agni, the earth belongs to Viṣṇu, and cows are daughters of the sun. / Whoever gives gold, a cow, and land attains an endless fruit from them.
He who accepts land and he who gives land— / both of them are doers of meritorious deeds and are destined for heaven.
Those men by whom land is unlawfully seized or caused to be seized— / stealing it or causing it to be stolen, they destroy their family to the seventh generation.
Whoever, dull-witted and enveloped in darkness, seizes it or causes it to be seized, / bound by the nooses of Varuṇa, is born in animal wombs.

6.32.s:
aśrubhiḥpatitaisteṣāṃdānānāmavakīrttanam
brāhmaṇasya hṛte kṣetre hataṃtripuruṣaṃ kulam
6.32.d:
अश्रुभिःपतितैस्तेषांदानानामवकीर्त्तनम्
ब्राह्मणस्य हृते क्षेत्रे हतंत्रिपुरुषं कुलम्
6.32.m: By the tears that fall from those [robbed], there is the scattering of gifts. / When the field of a brāhmaṇa is taken away, the family is destroyed for three generations.
Not by a thousand step-wells and wells, nor by a hundred horse sacrifices, / nor by the gift of ten million cows is a stealer of land purified.
Whatever has been performed, given, practiced as austerity, or studied, whatever is rooted in dharma, / is destroyed by the seizure of even half a finger's-width of boundary.
Having obstructed a cattle-crossing, a village roadway, a cremation ground, or a village, / one goes to hell until the dissolution of all beings.
A lie concerning a maiden slays five; a lie concerning cattle slays ten; / a lie concerning a horse slays a hundred; a lie concerning a man slays a thousand.
Telling a lie for the sake of gold, one slays those born and unborn; / telling a lie concerning land, one slays everything. Never tell a lie concerning land!

One should not take pleasure in the property of a brāhmaṇa, even if life-breaths have reached the throat. / Those scorched by fire sprout again; one scorched by a brāhmaṇa does not sprout.

Those scorched by fire sprout again, and likewise those scorched by the sun; / and even those struck down by a king’s punishment, but those struck down by a brāhmaṇa’s curse are completely destroyed.
Limbs nourished repeatedly by the property of a brāhmaṇa / crumble away at the time of need, just like a wall of sand.
A man committing the theft of a brāhmaṇa’s property goes to Raurava. / They say poison is not [real] poison: the property of a brāhmaṇa is said to be poison.
Poison slays only one person; the property of a brāhmaṇa slays sons and grandsons. / A man might digest iron powder, stone powder, or poison,
but what man in the three worlds will digest the property of a brāhmaṇa? / Whatever pleasure is derived from a brāhmaṇa’s property, whatever delight from a deity's property—
that wealth leads to the destruction of the family and becomes one's own ruin. / The property of a brāhmaṇa, the killing of a brāhmaṇa, and the wealth of a poor man,
as well as the gold of a guru or a friend, torments even one dwelling in heaven. / To a learned reciter of the Veda, well-born, poor, O Vāsava,
content, modest, endowed with all virtuous possessions, / distinguished by the study of the Vedas, austerity, knowledge, and restraint of the senses—
whatever is given to such a one, O best of gods, is indeed imperishable. / Just as milk, curd, ghee, and honey placed in an unbaked vessel
break the vessel due to its weakness, and yet the vessel is destroyed— / so an ignorant man who accepts a cow, gold, clothing, food, land, and sesame seeds
turns to ashes like a piece of wood. / Whoever constructs a new pond or excavates an old one,
uplifting his entire family, is honored in the heavenly world. / Step-wells, wells, ponds, and those arising in gardens,
when brought to renewal, yield the fruit of a pearl. / For him whose water remains during the summer season, O Vāsava,

He would never face danger, difficulty, or distress.
The water has stood for only a single day upon the earth, O best of gods.
it will save seven earlier and seven later generations of his family. / By giving the light of a lamp, that man becomes handsome.
By giving a sacrificial fee, he attains memory and intellect. / Even having committed a sinful act, he who gives to an appropriate recipient,
especially to a brāhmaṇa, is not tainted by sins. / When land, cows, or a servant are taken away by force,
whoever does not report it—they call him a slayer of a brāhmaṇa. / When a marriage, a sacrifice, or a gift is at hand, O Vāsava,
he who out of delusion causes an obstacle, when dead, is born as a worm. / Wealth bears fruit through charity; life bears fruit through protecting living beings.
One attains beauty, sovereignty, and freedom from disease as the fruit of non-violence. / One receives honor from eating fruits and roots; heaven is attained by truth.
From fasting unto death, one attains a kingdom and enjoys happiness everywhere. / One who is initiated into the rite of Śakra becomes rich in happiness; an eater of grass walks well.

One who bathes at the three junctures of the day becomes handsome; by drinking wind, he attains [the fruit of] a sacrifice. / He who bathes daily, endowed with the twilight worship and chanting of the Veda, becomes capable.
The harmless one goes to the realm of Virāj; fasting leads to the surface of heaven. / One who enters the fire is invariably glorified in the realm of Brahmā.
By abstaining from flavors, he gains cattle and sons. / And he who fasts lives long in heaven.
He who constantly sleeps on the bare ground attains his desired goal. / For one who practices the hero's posture, the hero's bed, and the hero's stance,
imperishable worlds are granted, moving wherever he desires. / Having observed fasting, initiation, and consecration, O Vāsava,
for twelve years, he surpasses the hero's stance. / Practicing purifying dharma, he is honored in the world of heaven.
For those best among the twice-born who recite this sacred teaching of Bṛhaspati, / four things increase: lifespan, knowledge, fame, and strength.
Nārada said: / This manual of dharma, composed by Bṛhaspati for Indra, / has been entirely declared to me, his devotee, by Maheśa, O king.

6.33.m: Nārada said: / How does the affliction caused by Saturn pass away? Tell me that, O best of gods! / As it is heard from your mouth, a creature is indeed freed thereby.
Mahādeva said: / Listen to the story, O divine sage, by which one is freed from bondage. / This king of planets among planets, the son of the Sun, is the lord of all.
Indeed, this celebrated god is a great planet having the form of Time, / with matted hair, diamond-like body hair, terrifying to the Dānavas.
And his narrative is not widely known in this world, O Lord. / It was specially kept secret by me and never spoken to anyone.
Formerly, in the lineage of Raghu, there was a king very famous named Daśaratha, / a universal monarch, a great hero, ruler of the seven continents.
Knowing Saturn to be at the end of Kṛttikā, he was indeed informed by the astrologers: / "Having pierced Rohiṇī, Saturn will now proceed.
The piercing of the cart [of Rohiṇī] is extremely fierce, causing terror to gods and asuras. / A most terrible famine will last for twelve years."
Then, having heard these words, the king, together with his ministers, / deliberated: "What is this dreadful danger that has approached?"
Seeing the world agitated—the citizens, country-folk, and others— / all the people everywhere were saying: "Destruction has arrived!"
The countries, along with cities and villages, were struck with fear on every side. / The king, self-controlled, asked the twice-born led by Vasiṣṭha:
"What remedy is there for this? Tell me indeed, O best of the twice-born!"
Vasiṣṭha said: / "This asterism belongs to Prajāpati; if that is pierced, whence can the subjects survive? / Indeed, this conjunction cannot be averted even by Brahmā, Indra, and the rest."

Thus thinking in his mind upon a supremely great deed of daring,
he took up a divine bow equipped with celestial weapons.
mounting his chariot, King Daśaratha went swiftly to the circle of the lunar mansions, / situated one hundred and twenty-five thousand yojanas above the sun.
Formerly, having positioned himself behind Rohiṇī, King Daśaratha, / in a divine golden chariot adorned with pearls and gems,
yoked with swan-colored horses, with a great banner raised high, / blazing with great jewels, radiant with his crest and crown,
shone then in the sky like a second sun. / Having drawn the bowstring up to the ear, he aimed the weapon of universal destruction.
Seeing the weapon of destruction, which causes terror to gods and demons, / smiling, through fear of it, the son of the Sun spoke these words:
Śani said: / "Your manly vigor, O lord of kings, strikes extreme fear into foes! / Gods, demons, humans, siddhas, vidyādharas, and serpents—
when looked upon by me, O king, they are reduced to ashes. / Pleased am I, O king of kings, with your penance and your valor! / Choose a boon; I will grant whatever you desire in your mind."
Daśaratha said: / "Having pierced Rohiṇī, you must never proceed, / as long as rivers, oceans, the moon, the sun, and the earth endure.
This is what was asked by me, O son of the Sun; I desire no other boon from you." / "So be it," said Śani, granting an eternal boon.
Pleased, he spoke yet again: "Choose a boon, O one of noble vows!" / Then, with a delighted mind, he prayed for another boon from Śani:
"The cart [of Rohiṇī] must not be pierced by you, O son of the Sun, / and a twelve-year famine must never be brought about!"
Śani said: / "A twelve-year famine will never take place, / and this fame of yours will traverse throughout the three worlds!"
Having obtained the two boons, his hair bristling with joy, the king, / laying down the bow on the chariot, with joined palms,
having meditated upon goddess Sarasvatī and Vināyaka, the lord of the ganas, / King Daśaratha then spoke this eulogy of the son of the Sun:

Daśaratha said: / "Homage to the black one, the blue one, and the one resembling the blue-throated [Śiva]; / homage to the one whose form is the fire of cosmic dissolution, and homage indeed to the ender of all [Yama]!
Homage to the one whose body is fleshless, having a long beard and matted hair; / homage to the large-eyed one, with a dried-up belly and a terrible form!
Homage to the one with a sturdy body, and homage indeed to the one with coarse hair; / homage to the tall one, to the withered one, O you with teeth of death, homage to you!
Homage to you with eyes in deep hollows, homage indeed to the one difficult to look upon; / homage to the dread, the fierce, the frightening, the skull-bearing one!
Homage to you, the all-devouring, homage to you with a wrinkled face; / O son of the Sun, homage to you, the giver of fearlessness to the suns!
Homage to you with downcast gaze, homage to you, the bringer of dissolution; / homage to you of slow gait, homage to the merciless one!
To the one whose body is burned by asceticism, and the one ever engaged in yoga; / homage to the one who is ever afflicted by hunger, and homage indeed to the insatiable!
O you whose eye is wisdom, homage to you, the son of the son of Kaśyapa! / Pleased, you grant universal rule; angered, you snatch it away in that very moment.
Gods, demons, and human beings, and siddhas, vidyādharas, and serpents, / when looked upon by you, all go to destruction from their very roots.
Bestow your grace upon me, O god! I have approached as one worthy of a boon." / Praised thus, then, the son of the Sun, the king of planets of mighty power,

with hair bristling with joy, that son of the Sun spoke words again: / "I am pleased, O king of kings, with this hymn of yours, O you of noble vows! / Choose a boon; I will grant it as you wish, O delight of the Raghus!"
Daśaratha said: / "From this day forward, O son of the Sun, no affliction should be caused by you / to gods, demons, humans, beasts, birds, or reptiles."
Śani said: / "They seize, therefore they are called planets (grahas); all planets are known to cause affliction. / Something impossible to give has been asked, O king; I will say what is fitting:
Whichever human being recites this hymn uttered by you, / once or twice a day, shall instantly become free from affliction."
To gods, asuras, humans, Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and Rākṣasas, / having reached death, I would give death in their fourth [house], at their birth, or at the end.
Furthermore, one who, endowed with faith, having become purified and composed, / worships an iron image of mine with leaves of the śamī tree,
and gives boiled rice mixed with black lentils and sesame, iron as the priestly fee, / and indeed a black cow or bull to a twice-born,
and on my day especially worships [me] with this praise, / and, having worshiped, recites the praise with folded hands,
I will never cause affliction to him, / whether in the transit, the natal ascendant, or in his planetary periods and sub-periods.
I will constantly protect him, and even the affliction of a planet [will be removed]; / by this very procedure the world will become freed from affliction.
In this manner, a boon was granted to you by me with reason, O descendant of Raghu! / Then, having obtained the three boons, King Daśaratha
deemed himself fulfilled, having bowed down to Śanaiścara. / And permitted by Śani, the swift king mounted his chariot,
and went to his own place; he then attained the highest good. / Whoever, having risen in the morning, recites this hymn on Saturday,
and whoever listens with faith to this praise while it is being recited, / that man is freed from sin and is honored in the heavenly realm.

6.34.m: Thirty-fourth chapter. / Nārada said: / Tell me particularly, O Lord of all, about the vow called Trispṛśā, / by hearing which people are freed in an instant from the bondage of karma.
Mahādeva said: / Hear about the great vow called Trispṛśā, which quells the flood of all sins, / destroys great sorrow, and is an incarnation of Kṛṣṇa.
It grants desires to those who have longing, but grants liberation to the desireless. / Hear, O brāhmaṇa, as I explain the vow called Trispṛśā.
Keśava has been worshipped visibly by him in the Kali age, / who constantly proclaims the Trispṛśā, O great sage.
When a preliminary rite is performed, there is destruction of all sins; / by the mere name of Trispṛśā [sin] is destroyed, there is no doubt about this.
Not by the Āgamas, not by the Purāṇas and others, not by sacrifices, nor by tens of millions of sacred fords, / nor by numerous collections of vows, even if gods are worshipped,
does liberation come about, O best of brāhmaṇas, if Trispṛśā is not observed. / For the sake of liberation, this Vaiṣṇava lunar day was perceived by the God of gods.
For twice-born people, Sāṃkhya is hard to know, especially in the Kali age; / there is no restraint of the senses, nor is there stability of mind.
For those separated from sense objects [only in theory], devoid of meditation and concentration, / and attached to desires and pleasures, Trispṛśā bestows liberation.
It was told in ancient times to me and to the four-faced [Brahmā] in the ocean, / in the Milk Ocean, by the Discus-bearer in the form of a Fish, to us who were bowed down [before him]:
“Those who will observe Trispṛśā, even if attached to sense objects, / liberation is granted by me even to them who are devoid of Sāṃkhya.”
Trispṛśā bestows liberation to those attached to desires and pleasures; / and it has been observed by numerous hosts of sages, O great sage.
If Trispṛśā occurs in the bright fortnight of Kārttika, / on a Monday or even a Wednesday, it destroys tens of millions of sins.
By fasting on which, the skull of Brahmā, which had stuck to the hand / of the great Lord tainted with murder, fell to the earth that very moment.
Freed from millions of torrents of Kali's impurities was the goddess who goes along three paths, / by the instruction of Mādhava, through fasting completely on Trispṛśā.
Eight murders had been committed previously by the valiant-armed [king], O great sage; / they vanished through the instruction of Bhṛgu, by fasting completely on Trispṛśā.
A brāhmaṇa was killed in the forest by Śatāyudha, O best of brāhmaṇas; / he was completely freed from the killing of a brāhmaṇa by fasting completely on Trispṛśā.
By the instruction of Bṛhaspati, Indra's sin arising from the murder of Namuci / was destroyed, O supreme among prominent sages, through fasting completely on Trispṛśā.
Sins such as the killing of a brāhmaṇa, through fasting completely on Trispṛśā, / go to dissolution, O best of brāhmaṇas; what to speak of other sins?
Neither at Prayāga, nor at Kāśī, nor at the Gomatī in the presence of Kṛṣṇa, / does liberation occur, O best of brāhmaṇas, if Trispṛśā is not observed.
And from dying at Prayāga, or at the Gomatī in the presence of Kṛṣṇa, / [or] by the mere bath in the Gomatī, eternal liberation occurs.
Even at home liberation comes about through fasting completely on Trispṛśā, / for one living among sense objects and endowed with desires and pleasures.
Even for one detached from sense objects, liberation is hard to attain through Sāṃkhya; / therefore, O best of brāhmaṇas, observe Trispṛśā, which bestows liberation.
Nārada said: / What is that great vow called Trispṛśā like, O best of gods, / which bestows liberation upon twice-born people, about which you have just spoken to me?
Mahādeva said: / That Trispṛśā was spoken in ancient times, O brāhmaṇa, to Jāhnavī by Mādhava / on the bank of the Prācī Sarasvatī out of compassion.
Jāhnavī said: / Burdened with millions of torrents of Kali's impurities, such as the killing of a brāhmaṇa, / people bathe in my water in the Kali age, O Hṛṣīkeśa.
By their hundreds of sins and defects, my body is made impure. / How will my sin depart, O Lord whose banner is Garuḍa?
Prācī-Mādhava said: / I shall tell you, there is no doubt; daughter, do not weep. / The dark banyan tree is my abode, and the goddess Prācī is before me.
The daughter of Brahmā flows [here]; having seen the queen of gods in front, / bathe [here] constantly; you will become purified here.
Where the Prācī, Brahmā's daughter, flows, there I am, without a doubt; / accompanied by hundreds of tens of millions of sacred fords, I dwell with the gods.
This holy abode, dear to me, destroys tens of millions of murders; / it was given by me, well-pleased, because you are dearer to me than my own life.
Tens of millions and thousands of sacred fords remain constantly, O Jāhnavī, / in the waters of the Prācī Sarasvatī at all times by my command.

From the killing of a brāhmaṇa, from the drinking of liquor, from the slaying of a cow, from the murder of a Śūdra woman, / from stealing the property of a brāhmaṇa, and likewise from failing to worship mother and father,
from riding in a vehicle, from treachery towards a guru, and from eating what should not be eaten, / from committing every sin, O daughter, the Prācī, Brahmā's daughter,
removes sins through a single bath in front of me. / Bathe, O best of rivers; you will become free from sin.
Jāhnavī said: / I am not able to come constantly, O Lord of gods; / tell me how sins are destroyed [otherwise], O Mādhava.
Prācī-Mādhava said: / Since you cannot come constantly, O Jāhnavī, / then I shall tell you something else, because you originated from my foot:
That which is superior to the Sarasvatī, superior to hundreds of tens of millions of sacred fords, / superior even to tens of millions of sacrifices, and superior to vows and gifts,
superior to recitation and fire-offerings, which bestows the fruit of the four aims of life, / and is superior to Sāṃkhya and Yoga—let auspicious Trispṛśā be observed!
In whichever month it arrives, whether in the bright or the dark [fortnight], / it should be observed, O best of rivers; when it is observed, one is freed from sin.
Jāhnavī said: / What is Trispṛśā like, O Lord? Tell me, O good Mādhava, / whose majesty of such a kind has just now been spoken by you to me.
When the tenth, eleventh, and Bhadrā [twelfth] lunar days occur on a single day, / is that Trispṛśā, O Lord, or otherwise? Tell me, O master!

Kṛṣṇa said:
O goddess, the Trispṛśā that was described by you is demonic; / it must be zealously avoided, just like a husband destitute of means.
Indeed, it is declared to belong to the asuras, destroying lifespan and strength; / it must be zealously avoided, just like a menstruating woman.
Just as a woman who abandons her own caste has gone to the lowest castes, / that very day of mine conjoined with the tenth lunar day is particularly to be discarded.
Just as ignorant men are defiled by contact with a menstruating woman, / even so my day conjoined with the tenth lunar day is defiled for men.
A Trispṛśā properly fasted upon destroys hundreds of myriads of slayings: / [when there is] the eleventh, the twelfth, and, at the close of the night, the thirteenth lunar day.
That alone is to be known as Trispṛśā, not one accompanied by the tenth lunar day. / Having committed a transgression, a man may be freed when an expiation is performed;
but I do not forgive the fault arising from overlap with the tenth lunar day, O river of the gods! / By him deadly poison has been consumed; he has eaten poison,
by whom the vow of the eleventh lunar day has been observed mixed with the tenth lunar day. / Considering this, my day should not be observed when conjoined with the tenth lunar day.
Merit acquired over ten million births and one's lineage go to destruction; / he causes his family to fall from heaven and leads them to Raurava and other hells.
Having purified one's own body, my day is certainly to be observed. / In case of extension [of the tithi], it is to be abandoned without overlap when conjoined with Śravaṇa and other [nakṣatras].
The merit of lifetimes goes to ruin for those who fast on the eleventh lunar day / when there is an extension [overlapping the tenth], especially when a doubt has arisen.
And by my command the twelfth lunar day, dear to me, is to be observed.

Jāhnavī said:
O Lord of the Universe, I shall observe the Trispṛśā according to your word; / freed from all sins, I shall become [pure] by your command.

The venerable Kṛṣṇa said:
Go to your own abode, auspicious one; you should never fear. / O goddess, best of rivers, sin will not attach to you.
Having bathed in the water of the Sarasvatī, those who worship Mādhava / and bow down to the Lord of the Universe go to the supreme destination.

Jāhnavī said:
Tell me the procedure, O Brahman! I shall perform it with all my possessions; / I shall propitiate the Lord of gods, the flawless Dāmodara.

Prācī-Mādhava said:
Listen, O goddess! I shall declare the ritual procedure of the Trispṛśā, / hearing which even a human being is freed from sins, O best of rivers!
A golden image of mine should be made with a pala, half a pala, / or even half of that, O river, according to the extent of one's wealth.
A copper vessel filled with sesame seeds should be prepared, / and a bright pot filled with water, endowed with the five gems,
encircled with garlands of flowers, perfumed with camphor and aloe; / then one should place Dāmodara [there], having bathed and anointed him.
Then clothing equipped with a pair of garments should be provided; / and worship should be performed with mantras proclaimed in the Purāṇas, / with seasonal, pure flowers and tender tulasī leaves.
One should offer a parasol along with a good pair of sandals to Viṣṇu, / and charming offerings of food, and very abundant fruits.
A sacred thread with an upper garment, new and firm, is to be given; / one should present a bamboo staff, well-shaped, reaching to the shoulder, and strong;
[Saying:] 'To Dāmodara', [he should worship] the two feet; 'To Mādhava', the two knees; / 'To the Granter of desires', the private parts; 'To the Vāmana form', the waist;
'To Padmanābha', the navel; 'To the Womb of the Universe', the belly; / 'To Him who is attained through knowledge', the heart; 'To the One who goes to Vaikuṇṭha', the throat;
'To the Thousand-armed', the two arms; 'To the Embodiment of Yoga', the two eyes. / Having worshipped properly with devotion, he should offer the argha according to the rules:
With a bright coconut placed upon a conch, / wrapped around with threads, held indeed in both hands:
'O Janārdana, since when remembered You always take away sins, / bad dreams, bad omens, and evils devised in the mind;
the fear of hell, O Lord, and the fear arising from misfortune / which might be mine, O Mahādeva, whether belonging to this world or the next;
by that [remembrance], O Lord of gods, protect me! Accept the argha, homage to You! / May Your glance of grace ever rest upon me, O Dāmodara!'
Then he should offer incense, a lamp, and food offerings, and perform the waving of lamps. / O best of rivers, he should circle the lotus over the head of Hari.
Having performed this rite, he should then worship his own guru. / He should give gold, garments, a turban, and a tunic,
shoes too, an umbrella, a ring, and a water-pot, / a meal, betel leaf, the seven grains, and a priestly gift.
Having worshipped the guru [and] the Lord of gods, he should keep a night-vigil for Hari / accompanied by song and dance, and likewise accompanied by sacred scriptures.
And at the end of the night, having offered argha to the god according to rule / and performed rites such as bathing, he should eat together with the brāhmaṇas.
Śiva said: / O twice-born one, this wonderful, hair-raising narrative of Trispṛśā, / upon merely hearing it, one obtains the merit arising from bathing in the Gaṅgā.
The fruit of a thousand horse sacrifices and hundreds of Vājapeya sacrifices, / that fruit one completely attains by fasting on Trispṛśā.
The father's side, the mother's side, and likewise his own side: / liberated together with all of them, he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
Whatever merit is in crores of sacred bathing-places, whatever fruit is in crores of sacred fields, / that fruit one completely attains by fasting on Trispṛśā.
Whatever brāhmaṇas observe it, kṣatriyas whose minds are on Kṛṣṇa, / vaiśyas, or those born of śūdra wombs, and likewise those of other castes,
they all attain liberation, having left this earth, O best of the twice-born. / Just as the twelve-syllable mantra is the king of mantras among mantras,
so too is this [vow] among vows, which Trispṛśā was performed / formerly by Brahmā, and afterwards performed by royal sages.
What need to speak of others, my child? Trispṛśā is the giver of liberation. / The vow arising from Trispṛśā according to this rule, O brāhmaṇa,
the man who performs it with devotion—listen, I shall declare its fruit: / The fruit, O brāhmaṇa, that comes from plunging into the Gaṅgā at Vārāṇasī
through thousands of manvantaras, that belongs to the performer of Trispṛśā. / The fruit that comes from bathing in the eastern Yamunā over crores of years,
that fruit a man performing the Trispṛśā vow fully attains. / That fruit [gained] at Kurukṣetra over crores of solar eclipses
through gifts of hundreds of loads of gold, is [attained] by performing Trispṛśā. / Thousands of crores of sins and hundreds of crores of killings
are reduced to ashes swiftly by a single fast. / This vow of Trispṛśā provides a refuge for the refugeless;
even those with hundreds of great sins desire refuge [through it], O brāhmaṇa-sage. / It was spoken by Kṛṣṇa Himself before the son of Parāśara.
And if someone, having written down this Vaiṣṇava [narrative], reveals it to a twice-born, / even if strung with hordes of sins, he will attain liberation.
Even through merit over hundreds of manvantaras, O wise one, / Trispṛśā is hard to obtain in this world; it is rarely attained by mortals.
Those vile men who, having found Trispṛśā in the Kali age, do not observe it, / the fruit of their birth and their very life will be in vain.

6.34.m:
The state of a ghost has been crossed over by those, without śrāddhas and without sons, / by whom Trispṛśā was performed even once, O wise one, having obtained it in the Kali yuga.

Thirty-fifth Chapter. / Mahādeva said: / Next, I shall tell you about the unsurpassed Unmīlanī, / by the mere hearing of which, from the bondage of the cycle of birth,

a sinful soul is freed from sins and is glorified in the heavenly world; / deities and ancestors alike attain its course.

One seeking learning obtains learning; one obtains all desires; / through the vow of it, without doubt, he is glorified in the heavenly world.

Indeed, having attained his own abode there, he is glorified in the world of Śiva. / Therefore, O king, do you perform the worship of the Vaiṣṇavas?

Those who constantly serve Vaiṣṇavas, O king— / do you impose punishment on them, or does the ruler of men not [punish] them?

O king, one who eats after they have eaten— / by them alone is Viṣṇu worshipped, by whom He is worshipped with devotion.

Having placed on your head every day the Śālagrāma stone, / do you, O king, constantly wear it on your neck with great devotion?

Do you, O king, faithfully enjoy the remains of the incense of Viṣṇu? / Having always performed the waving of lights, O king, do you offer it to the devotees?

6.34.m:
Having waved the conch-water with devotion over the head of Hari, / do you constantly carry it on your head and bestow the remainder upon the Vaiṣṇavas?

Having daily prepared food offering endowed with all ingredients, / and having given it to Viṣvaksena, do you yourself eat it, O brāhmaṇa?

And is the food offered to Viṣṇu eaten together with the Vaiṣṇavas? / Do you daily praise Janārdana with devotion using the thousand names?

Do you offer lamps and argha to Viṣṇu, and perform singing and dancing? / Do you worship the One worthy of worship with shoots of śyāmā grass, O best of kings?

Worship with shoots of śyāmā grass, my child, is always very hard to obtain. / Merit equal to the gift of the earth [is gained] when worship is performed with dūrvā grass.

Therefore, indeed, there is nothing like dūrvā grass in this world, on earth. / Worship should certainly be done with it by one desiring intimate union with Viṣṇu.

Therefore, do you constantly perform worship with dūrvā grass? / Or do you especially perform worship with barley grains and unbroken rice?

Fortnight after fortnight, O best of kings, the Dvādaśī vow according to rule, / which, when performed, O great king, destroys great sins,

bestows liberation, grants happiness, and always bestows long life— / this is declared as the vow of Viṣṇu, bestowing liberation upon the Vaiṣṇavas,

the king is tainted by that sin and becomes an inhabitant of hell. / Having abandoned the fourfold overlap and fasted on the day of Hari, / raising up ten million ancestors, he is honored in the world of Viṣṇu.

Gautama said:
Listen, O king! I shall declare the great vow named Vaiṣṇava, / hearing which all sinners attain liberation that very instant.

The merit arising from the twelfth lunar day has not been declared by me to anyone.

You are a Vaiṣṇava, O great king, a devotee devoted to the Lord among men; / listen to that vow, a great mystery of the Vaiṣṇavas.

Formerly, by devotion, [the vow] named Unmīlanī was told to me / by Mādhava when he was well pleased; I declare it to you, O king.

[When] the eleventh lunar day lasts day and night and extends a ghaṭikā into the dawn, / that is to be known as Unmīlanī, especially dear to Hari.

Whatever holy places and sacred shrines there are in the three worlds, / along with sacrifices, Vedas, and austerities, are equal to only a ten-millionth part of it.

There was nothing equal to Unmīlanī, nor will there ever be: / not Prayāga, nor Kurukṣetra, nor Kāśī, nor Puṣkara;
